items.title: Bounded or Boundless? Four More Variants, and a Glance at Seven Annihilationist Cousins

items.zh: 又若計命即是身者，彼計我是色。若計命異於身者，彼計我非色。若計我俱遍，無二無缺者，彼計我亦是色亦非色。若為對治此故，即於此義中，由異句異文而起執者，彼計我非色非非色。又若見少色、少非色者，彼計有邊。若見彼無量者，彼計有無邊。若復遍見，而色分少、非色分無量，或色分無量、非色分少者，彼計亦有邊亦無邊。若為對治此故，但由文異，不由義異，而起執者，彼計非有邊非無邊。
items.en: Further, those who see a limited amount of form, and a limited amount of what is formless, hold the self to be bounded. Those who see these as boundless hold the self to be boundless. Those who see form as limited but the formless as boundless, or form as boundless but the formless as limited, hold the self to be both bounded and boundless. And those who, merely to answer this last position with different wording rather than any different meaning, arrive at a further position hold the self to be neither bounded nor boundless.

items.zh: 或計解脫之我，遠離二種。
items.en: Some, further, hold that the self, once liberated, is entirely free of both these categories.

items.title: Refuting the Atomists: Observation Finds No Permanent Atom, Anywhere

items.zh: 又計極微常住論者，我今問汝，隨汝意答。汝為觀察計極微常？為不觀察計彼常耶？若不觀察者，離慧觀察，而定計常，不應道理。若言已觀察者，違諸量故，不應道理。
items.en: Further, to those who hold atoms to be permanent: I now ask you, answer as you see fit — do you hold atoms to be permanent through actual observation, or without any observation at all? If without observation, then reaching a firm conclusion of permanence apart from any discerning examination makes no sense. If through observation, then your conclusion contradicts every recognised means of valid knowledge — this too makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？諸微塵性為由細故，計彼是常？為由與麁果物其相異故，計彼常耶？若由細者，離散損減，轉復羸劣，而言是常，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: do you hold atoms permanent because they are subtle, or because their characteristic differs from the gross object they compose? If because they are subtle, then note that once dispersed and diminished, they grow only weaker and less capable — yet you call precisely this weakening, diminishing thing "permanent," which makes no sense.

items.zh: 若言由相異故者，是則極微超過地水火風之相，不同種類相故，而言能生彼類果，不應道理。又彼極微，更無異相可得，故不中理。
items.en: If because their characteristic differs from the gross object, then atoms would have to lie entirely outside the character of earth, water, fire, and wind altogether, belonging to a wholly different kind — yet you also claim they produce precisely that kind of result, which makes no sense. And, further, no such distinct characteristic for atoms is ever actually found apart from the gross matter itself — so this does not hold up either.

items.title: Whether Identical or Different, Dispersed or Combined — Atoms Still Fail

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？從諸極微所起麁物，為不異相？為異相耶？若言不異相者，由與彼因無差別故，亦應是常；是則應無因果決定，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: is the gross object arising from atoms identical in character to them, or different? If identical, then since it has no distinguishing feature apart from its cause, it too should be permanent — yet this would erase any determinate distinction between cause and effect at all, which makes no sense.

items.zh: 若異相者，汝意云何？為從離散極微，麁物得生？為從聚集耶？若言從離散者，應一切時一切果生；是則應無因果決定，不應道理。
items.en: If different, then what do you think: does the gross object arise from atoms while they are dispersed, or only once they are gathered together? If while dispersed, then every result should arise at every single moment without exception — which again erases any determinate cause-and-effect relation, and makes no sense.

items.zh: 若從聚集者，汝意云何？彼麁果物從極微生時，為不過彼形質之量？為過彼形質量耶？若言不過彼形質量者，從形質分物，生形質有分物，不應道理。
items.en: If only once gathered together, then consider: does the resulting gross object exceed the spatial extent of its constituent atoms, or not? If it does not exceed it, then something imperceptible and indivisible (the atom) is said to produce something perceptible and divisible (the gross object) while occupying exactly the same space — this makes no sense.

items.zh: 若言過者，諸極微體無細分故，不可分析，所生麁物亦應是常，亦不中理。若復說言，有諸極微，本無今起者，是則計極微常，不應道理。
items.en: If it does exceed it, then since atoms, by definition, have no further parts and cannot be analysed any further, the gross object produced beyond that extent should, by the same reasoning, likewise be permanent — this too fails to hold up. And if you then say that, in the space beyond, further atoms simply arise where none existed before, then to hold that atoms are permanent makes no sense.

items.title: No Analogy Fits, and Gross Objects Only Ever Appear Because Someone Needs Them

items.zh: 又汝何所欲？彼諸極微，起造麁物，為如種子等？為如陶師等耶？若言如種子等者，應如種子，體是無常。若言如陶師等者，彼諸極微應有思慮，如陶師等，不應道理。若不如種等及陶師等者，是則同喻不可得故，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you actually intend: do atoms give rise to gross objects the way a seed gives rise to a sprout, or the way a potter shapes clay? If like a seed, then, like a seed, atoms should themselves be impermanent. If like a potter, then atoms would have to be capable of deliberation, the way a potter is — which makes no sense. And if neither analogy applies, then no comparable example whatsoever can be found to support your claim — which likewise makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝意云何？諸外物起，為由有情？為不爾耶？若言由有情者，彼外麁物由有情生，所依細物不由有情，不應道理。誰復於彼制其功能？若言不由有情者，是則無用，而外物生，不應道理。
items.en: Further, what do you think: does the arising of external objects depend on sentient beings, or not? If it does, then while the gross external object depends on beings for its production, the subtle atoms it rests on supposedly do not — this makes no sense; who, then, governs the atoms' own capacity to produce it? If it does not depend on beings at all, then external objects would have to arise with no purpose or need behind them whatsoever — which likewise makes no sense.

items.zh: 如是隨念諸蘊有情故，由一境界一切識流不斷絕故，由想及受變不變故，計彼前際及計後際常住論者，不應道理。又由觀察不觀察故，由共相故，由自相故，由起造故，根本所用故，極微常論不應道理。是故計常論者非如理說。
items.en: Thus, because of recollecting the aggregates as a being, because the whole stream of consciousness with one object is not cut off, and because perception and feeling change or do not change, the doctrine of permanence held by those who speculate about the past and the future does not accord with reason. Further, because of observation and non-observation, because of the shared characteristic, because of the particular characteristic, because of production, and because of what the root is used for, the doctrine that atomic particles are permanent does not accord with reason. Therefore the doctrine of permanence is not soundly reasoned.

items.title: Genuine Permanence Requires No Change at All, Anywhere, Ever — and Doctrine Five, and Fascicle 6, Close

items.zh: 我今當說常住之相。若一切時無變異相，若一切種無變異相，若自然無變異相，若由他無變異相。又無生相，當知是常住相。
items.en: I shall now state the true mark of permanence. It is the mark of undergoing no change at any time whatsoever; the mark of undergoing no change in any respect whatsoever; the mark of being naturally, inherently unchanging; and the mark of never being changed by anything else. Further, the mark of never arising at all should likewise be understood as the mark of true permanence.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 6 finishes the doctrine of permanence: variants that say the self is bounded or boundless, and the atomists' claim that atoms are permanent. It closes with a definition of what real permanence would have to be, which turns out to describe only the unconditioned.

Missing from Ru-Yi's translation (0308b28–c04), now supplied in our own: a summary sentence restating why those who reckon past and future as permanent are mistaken (memory recalls aggregates, consciousness does not continue unbroken on one object, perception and feeling change), and that their view comes from observing in some respects and not in others.

Some hold the self is bounded (Venerable Miào Jìng: "as big as a mustard seed, or a finger", or the size of the body), some boundless, some both, some neither, "differing only in wording, not meaning". The treatise lists these briefly, with a glance at seven forms of annihilationism, and moves on.

The atomists hold that atoms are permanent and combine into gross things, which are impermanent. Do they hold this by observation or without it? Without observation, a firm conclusion "apart from any discerning examination makes no sense". With observation, it contradicts the means of knowledge. Master Cháng Bǎi: perception cannot see atoms; inference cannot show they are permanent; and scripture says atoms are posited by analysis, which is Day 16's point: the atom is a limit of analysis, not a building block.

subs.head: Dispersed or combined, atoms still fail

blocks.text: If gross things arise from dispersed atoms, "every result should arise at every moment". Venerable Miào Jìng: the outsiders say atoms lie scattered in space during the empty eon; if scattered atoms could produce things, a world should form during the empty eon too. If atoms combine, they must change, and so are not permanent.

subs.head: The world arises because of beings

blocks.text: The treatise asks why gross things appear at all, and answers that they appear because beings need and use them. Venerable Miào Jìng draws out a central principle: "All worlds in the ten directions have beings as their basis, and beings have mind as theirs; that is Buddhist doctrine." And: "Buddhist teaching centres on human life; it is not a cosmology." This is the same point made on Days 8 and 11: the world is the shared result of beings' karma, so its explanation starts from mind, not from particles.

The fascicle ends by defining the true mark of permanence: "undergoing no change at any time whatsoever; in any respect whatsoever; being naturally, inherently unchanging; never being changed by anything else; and never arising." Nothing that arises meets this definition. Only the unconditioned (Day 21) does, and the unconditioned does not cause anything.

Five of the sixteen doctrines have been examined: effect in the cause, manifestation by conditions, the reality of past and future, a self, and permanence. Each time, the treatise grants a real observation (continuity, memory, the stability of matter) and shows that it is explained better by impermanent, conditioned processes. Yogācāra's own picture (seeds, imprints, conventional selves, karma as present potential) has been sharpened against each opponent. Fascicle 7 continues with the remaining eleven doctrines, beginning with the view that everything is caused by past karma.

quiz.q: The text describes bounded, boundless, both, and finally "neither — differing only in wording, not meaning." How do the teachers explain this?
options: "bounded" is a self as small as a mustard seed or finger, or body-sized; the fourth merely inverts the third — different words, same meaning
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Clinging to a self as big as a mustard seed — that's 'limited form' — or as big as a finger." Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Vibhāṣā*: "a self dwelling in the body, the same size as the body"; "'not bounded' is 'also boundless,' 'not boundless' is 'also bounded' — the prior wording reversed, the meaning the same."

quiz.q: The text first asks the atomists whether they hold atoms permanent by observation or without. What fault does each answer bring?
options: without observation, a firm conclusion apart from examination makes no sense; with observation, it contradicts the means of knowledge
quiz.why: "If without observation, then reaching a firm conclusion of permanence apart from any discerning examination makes no sense. If through observation, then your conclusion contradicts every recognised means of valid knowledge." The next question shows how.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, how does holding atoms permanent "contradict the means of knowledge"?
options: perception doesn't see atoms; inference can't conclude they're permanent; scripture says atoms are posited by analysis — provisional
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Perception can't see atoms; inference by reflection can't conclude they're permanent; scripture says atoms are posited by analytic insight — provisional." Venerable Miào Jìng: "As for scripture, the Buddha never said atoms are permanent."

quiz.q: If gross objects arise from dispersed atoms, "every result should arise at every moment." How does Venerable Miào Jìng reason?
options: outsiders say atoms scatter in space in the empty eon; if scattered atoms could produce, the empty eon should already form a world
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "If they have this power in the formation eon, they should have it in the empty eon too." The text: "every result should arise at every single moment … which again erases any determinate cause-and-effect relation." Master Cháng Bǎi: atoms spread through space would produce every result at all times — no determinate causality.

quiz.q: The text asks whether external things arise because of sentient beings. What core Buddhist point does Venerable Miào Jìng draw from this?
options: all worlds have beings as their basis, and beings have mind as theirs — Buddhism is a teaching about life, not a cosmology
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "All worlds in the ten directions have beings as their basis, and beings have mind as theirs — that is Buddhist doctrine"; "Buddhist teaching centres on human life, not cosmology." Master Cháng Bǎi: external things arise from beings' shared karma and needs — cups and chairs get made because someone needs them.

quiz.q: In closing, how does the treatise define the true mark of permanence?
options: no change at any time or in any respect, by nature or by anything else; and never arising
quiz.why: "It is the mark of undergoing no change at any time whatsoever; … in any respect whatsoever; … being naturally, inherently unchanging; and … never being changed by anything else. Further, the mark of never arising at all." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Only what doesn't arise is permanent; whatever arises must cease"; "complete liberation is called the mark of non-arising." A is mere Īṣīkā-like firmness, not true permanence.
